h1:
Pai Walking Street After Dark
Walk, Eat, Grilled Skewers, Sweets & Crafts
intro: Once the sun drops and the air cools, Rangsiyanon Road in central Pai closes to traffic and turns into a walking street that opens almost every night, running on into Chaisongkhram Road. Both sides fill up with grill carts, banana roti, khao soi, sweets and fruit smoothies, mixed in with handmade craft stalls and hand-screened T-shirts. This guide walks you through what time to show up, which foods are worth hunting down, roughly what they cost, and which crafts are worth carrying home — plus honest tips on everything from the drive up to Pai to the stalls that still don't take QR payments.

blocks.html: Pai Walking Street isn't sprawling like the night markets in bigger cities, but its charm is in how laid-back it feels and the mix of people — Thais, northerners, and the foreign travelers who come to stay for weeks. The food follows suit: Thai street food, local northern dishes, and Western options like falafel and veggie burgers run by foreigners who settled here. Walking the whole strip takes about half an hour to an hour if you keep stopping to taste things.

blocks.text: Where is Pai Walking Street, and what time does it open?

items: Location — The main stretch runs along Rangsiyanon Road in central Pai, then carries on into Chaisongkhram Road, all walkable. It's the area where the guesthouses, cafes and bars cluster.
Opening hours — Stalls start setting up around 5pm, most are open by 6pm, and it's busiest from 7–9pm. Most begin packing up around 10pm.
Open almost daily — Unlike walking streets in many towns that only run on weekends, Pai opens nearly every night. But in low season or on rainy nights there are noticeably fewer stalls.
Length — About 1km, an easy stroll with no need to rush.

blocks.title: Honest note about the drive up to Pai
blocks.html: The Chiang Mai–Pai road has 762 mountain curves in total. If you get carsick easily, take motion-sickness pills before you set off and sit up front. If you're riding a motorbike yourself, be extra careful — the road is winding, steep and slick in places when it rains. By the time you reach Pai for the walking street, plenty of people are already worn out, so give yourself a little time to recover from the drive before you head out to eat.

blocks.text: What to eat as you walk

blocks.html: Food on Pai Walking Street is cheaper than many people expect — most things run from around ten-something baht to under a hundred per item. Here they are in the order I'd try them, starting with grilled skewers to snack on and ending with something sweet.

items.name: Grilled skewers (pork skewers, grilled chicken, sai ua)
items.blurb: The star of Pai Walking Street. Charcoal-grill carts line up and send the smell down the whole road — pork skewers, grilled chicken, northern herb sausage (sai ua) and hill-tribe-style marinated grills. Easy to grab a skewer and nibble as you walk.

items.name: Khao soi
items.blurb: The northern dish to try now that you're in the region — egg noodles in a coconut-curry broth with northern curry paste, topped with crispy fried noodles, with chicken or beef, a squeeze of lime and pickled greens. Some spots in the area have sit-down bowls, others box it up so you can carry it.

items.name: Pad thai & stir-fried noodles
items.blurb: Fresh-prawn pad thai stir-fried hot in the wok right at the front of the stall, boxed up to eat as you go. A favorite with foreign travelers and easy to find all along the strip.

items.name: Fried & steamed dumplings
items.blurb: The crispy-bottomed fried dumpling stall is a Pai Walking Street favorite where people queue up. Well-stuffed and good with the dipping sauce — a fun snack, available fried or steamed.

items.name: Falafel & veggie burgers
items.blurb: Pai has a lot of long-stay foreign travelers, so Western and vegetarian stalls are tucked into the walking street — falafel wraps, veggie burgers and vegan dishes. Good if you don't eat meat.

items.name: Fried skewers & fried meatballs
items.blurb: Fried meatballs, battered squid and fried sausage on skewers with dipping sauce — something to hold and snack on while you browse the craft stalls, and about the cheapest thing on the strip.

items.name: Som tam, yam & Isan food
items.blurb: The spicy corner of the street — papaya salad pounded fresh, mixed yam, grilled pork neck. Sit at a roadside table and make it a proper meal; with a cold beer it suits the atmosphere even more.

items.name: Banana roti & egg roti
items.blurb: The classic walking-street sweet, fried fresh at the stall, drizzled with condensed milk and chocolate, with banana or egg — buttery, crisp outside and soft inside. Kids and adults both love it.

items.name: Banana grilled in banana leaf (Grandma's stall)
items.blurb: A local sweet that regular visitors pass along to each other — banana grilled over charcoal wrapped in banana leaf, with that smoky banana-leaf aroma. You won't find it everywhere, so if you spot Grandma's stall, try a skewer.

items.name: Mango sticky rice & Thai sweets
items.blurb: Mango sticky rice with coconut cream, khanom krok, banana-leaf-wrapped Thai sweets and coconut ice cream — several stalls to choose from to finish the meal.

items.name: Thai iced tea, coffee & fruit smoothies
items.blurb: Cool off as you walk with iced tea, milk tea, blended coffee and big cups of fresh fruit smoothies. Some stalls serve a whole pineapple with a straw — photogenic and refreshing.

items.name: Cocktail carts & draft beer
items.blurb: In the evening, cocktail carts and tiny bars pop up along the strip — mocktails and cocktails at easy prices, good to carry on with or sip while listening to live music at a bar nearby.

blocks.title: Carry plenty of cash
blocks.html: Most cart vendors on Pai Walking Street are cash-first. Some have PromptPay QR but not all do, and the mobile signal in parts of Pai isn't great, so scans can be slow to go through. Bring lots of small notes (20–100 baht) and you'll move faster. Most food sits in the 10–120 baht range per item.

Another part of Pai Walking Street's charm is the handmade crafts tucked between the food stalls. Many vendors make and sell their own work — northerners, hill-tribe makers, and artists who moved to Pai and settled in. Some of it you won't find in the bigger cities, so walk slowly and you'll come across something you like.

items.name: Hill-tribe textiles & cloth bags
items.blurb: Hand-woven tribal-pattern fabric, cloth bags, scarves and Pai-style clothing in bold colors. You can sometimes haggle a little, especially near closing time.

items.name: Silverwork & handmade jewelry
items.blurb: Earrings, bangles, rings and beadwork, made one piece at a time — some vendors work right at the stall while you watch. Good for small, light souvenirs.

items.name: Soap, essential oils & herbal goods
items.blurb: Handmade soap bars, essential oils, scented candles and products from local herbs, with natural scents — good souvenirs that won't weigh down your bag.

items.name: Hand-screened tees & art
items.blurb: Hand-screened Pai-design T-shirts, hand-drawn postcards, paintings and small home pieces from artists living in Pai — souvenirs that genuinely carry the feel of this town.

blocks.title: On haggling
blocks.html: Food prices are fixed and not up for negotiation, but crafts, clothing and souvenirs can be haggled a little, politely. If you're buying several pieces, try asking for a bundle price. Most vendors are friendly and easy to talk to — but don't push the price down too far, since many pieces are handmade and take a long time.

blocks.text: What time to go, and what to know before you do

items: The golden window — Drop by around 6–7pm: most stalls are open, food hasn't run out, and it's not yet at its most packed. After 9pm some vendors start packing up.
Allow 1.5–2 hours — if you want to eat your way through, browse the crafts, and sit with live music at a roadside bar along the way.

On the weather — Pai sits in a valley, so nights are cooler than you'd think, especially in the cold season — bring a light jacket. As for the morning sea of fog, it depends on the weather: some days it's there, some days it isn't, so don't count on seeing it every time.

March–April — This is the burning-season haze in northern Thailand. Visibility can be murky and the air isn't great. If you're sensitive to dust, bring a mask and check the air-quality numbers before you plan.
Parking — The walking street closes to traffic in the evening, so you'll park on the outskirts and walk in, or just walk from your in-town guesthouse, which most of the time is close by anyway.

faq.q: What days and times is Pai Walking Street open?
faq.a: Pai Walking Street on Rangsiyanon Road opens almost every night. Stalls start setting up around 5pm, most are open by 6pm, and it's busiest from 7–9pm, with vendors packing up around 10pm. In low season or on rainy nights there are fewer stalls than usual.

faq.q: Roughly how much does food on Pai Walking Street cost?
faq.a: Grilled and fried skewers run about ฿10–30 each, pad thai or other one-plate dishes around ฿40–60, khao soi about ฿50–70, banana roti around ฿30–50, and drinks ฿25–60 per cup. Most stalls take cash, so bring plenty of small notes.

faq.q: What crafts are sold on Pai Walking Street?
faq.a: You'll find hand-woven tribal-pattern fabric, cloth bags, silverwork and handmade jewelry, soap and essential oils from local herbs, plus hand-screened T-shirts and art from artists living in Pai. Many vendors make and sell their own work, and you can haggle a little, politely.

faq.q: Is the drive up to Pai scary, and does it make you carsick?
faq.a: The Chiang Mai–Pai road has 762 mountain curves. If you get carsick easily, take motion-sickness pills before you set off and sit up front. If you're riding a motorbike yourself, be careful — the road is winding, steep and slick when it rains. Once you arrive, rest until the carsickness passes before heading out to the walking street.

faq.q: When's the best time to visit Pai, and do I need to watch out for haze?
faq.a: The best weather is in the cool season, roughly November to February — pleasant and cool. The morning sea of fog depends on the weather and isn't there every day. March to April is the burning-season haze, when visibility can turn murky, so if you're sensitive to dust, bring a mask and check the air-quality numbers before you go.
